en: Had looked and set eyes on him.
Growing to maturity, becoming a hero,
Becoming equal to the sons of the people,
He began a clash with the governor.
Those who went he laid sprawling
And slaughtered to the last.
Clouds gathered in the sky.
That bastard, wretched Jakyp
Escaped and went to the Kyrgyz.
Manas is no ordinary boy,
No slave who gives an easy way.
The Burut's affairs were like flowers,
It was the time when they were thriving.
In the fortress of Great Beijing,
When the New Year month came,
I saw a sign of him.
If the reckoning fits, that was
The time when he was being born.
Wind rose, the lake heaved,
Clouds were lashed across the sky
And reached down, enclosing the earth.
Rain fell for eighty days;
Upon Kakan-Chin's Beijing,
An earthquake came.
It seems it was Manas himself;
The blue-maned blood-drinker, then,
Was being born!
Manas is no ordinary boy;
If he turns back and attacks,
He is no slave who will let us prosper!
To Kakan-Chin's Beijing,
To Karykan himself,
Provide six swift horses,
Provide a palm-sized letter.
Send a letter flying to Karykan.
If you send it flying, send it swiftly.
Blood-drinking Manas, that Burut,
Will tirelessly migrate and find land,
Will somehow go and find a people.
He will watch Kakan and scout the roads.
He is no boy who will fail to prepare,
No slave who will fail to fight.
To Beijing of Kakan-Chin,
He will return and attack.
Braid the thoroughbred's mane;
Within five or six years,
See him in your Beijing!
Of forty-doored Beijing,
Gathering many of these people,
Of the strong men in sleeveless coats,
Gathering every one,
From the mighty men with rank buttons on their caps,
Let us gather the finest.
Of the khans wearing arm guards,
Let us gather all, leaving none.
Of the young, growing boys,
Let us gather all, leaving none.
The great magician at Zuu-Kuduk,
His skill in discernment is considerable;
Let us bring the great magician.
To the Chinese, the people of forty khans,
Let us send word to all together.
Their great lords, their chiefs,
Their elders, their people,
Their young, growing boys,
Let us gather them all together.
Before the discerning men,
Let us make them pass in file.
From the skillful spearmen,
From the mighty, brave-hearted men,
Who will clash with Karakan
And fight without fleeing,
Let us find courageous heroes.
Setting a thorough watch,
Let us safeguard our lives well.
I have property in many places.
At the seat of Great Beijing,
Among Karykan's great plane trees,
In the garden where he goes to stroll,
Made to scout the face of the earth,
Trained thoroughly for watch duty,
There is a red fox forty fathoms long.
Let us set a watch upon the rise;
Let us fortify and guard our lives.
The burly one among the young men,
Of the One-Eyed people, the great
Wrestler Mamytbek—
Let us set him on watch.
Let us set a wild ram on watch;
Let us guard our wretched lives.
Manas is no ordinary boy.
Unless we take thought and guard our lives,
He is no slave who gives an easy way.
I heard accounts from those who came,
I traced them through tradition,
I asked the knowing men.
Alöökö's youngest,
The warrior of sixty noblemen—
A glowing ember was born from the hearth.
This year he must have turned twelve,
His mighty son called Kongurbay.
When he reached the age of seven,
He penned the governors in.
Of the Chinese with red tassels,
He beat their mighty men.
Unable to bear his unruliness,
The people of Great Beijing grew weary.
He had so many mules slaughtered.
When Karykan approved of him,
He had him named Hero Kongurbay.
He made him a house built on the upland;
He is an imposing champion, they say,
Who lays low those he meets.
Because he trusted him, Karykan
Made him a mighty khan over the monks.
Kakan knows his heroism, they say.
Against the enemy who presses down,
At the edge of a people facing slaughter,
‘He will guard the people without wavering,’
He deems him suited, they say.
Making him a man of greater spiritual power,
Making him khan of Great Beijing,
That grim-looking hero Kongurbay,
Let us bring him here.
Of the ill-omened Burut,
Let us set him squarely in the path!
He is the hero renowned in combat;
To match Khan Manas,
He is the lion sprung from Beijing.
I have heard his fame from everyone.
He is skillful among spearmen, they say.
The enemy's stratagems,
He is a mighty man who knows them thoroughly.
Those he takes into his wrath,
If he grapples, he sweeps them down, they say.
If an army worth the whole world comes,
If it comes so vast the earth splits,
Entering alone, he swallows it up, they say.
The khans wearing arm guards,
He made pass in file, they say.
Sixty Chinese, countless governors,
He took as close companions, they say.
Karagul, Katal's son,
This one is a dark omen.
He is the one who goes on patrol.
He cut a spear from reed, they say.
Of firm-backed Beijing,
He gathered the champions, they say.
Let us set a strong watch.
Let us send word to the governor.
At Kakan-Chin's frontier,
The fiercely wrathful infidel,
The warrior Khan Kongurbay,
Let us raise him as khan.
He is the support we rely upon,
He is the place to shelter securely,
Flourishing Beijing and great Kakan,
He is the hero who will guard them!
Let us send word to the governor.
The younger brother of sixty noblemen,
Alöökö's youngest,
Let us settle him at Chong-Tabylgy,
Have him set a wild ram on watch,
Of Chin-Machin and Beijing,
Have him watch and scout the roads.
Orokkyr and Muzkindik,
Have those brought,
Have a strict watch kept.
Unless we guard our precious lives,
Unless we keep the land patrolled,
Unless we fortify and make it secure,
Any man who comes against us,
Unless we seize and slaughter him,
Unless we establish a strong watch,
Unless we carry out this plan,
Unless we gather a great army like this,
He is no boy who gives an easy way;
Manas is no ordinary slave!”
Speaking many counsels, Esenkan
Had sent word to his khan.
Not abandoning what he had said,
Setting Beijing thundering,
He had gathered it all.
The war drums were beaten hard.
The many seething great lords,
Before one could say this or that,
Before an eye could open and close,
The tent with golden pillars,
They had loaded on his mule,
And brought in
The warrior, hero Kongurbay.
Kayoboz, riding a mule,
A great lord of the vast Chinese people,
Clad him in a governor's robe
And now set him on watch.
One who brought news if a wind stirred,
The cunning duck with copper wings,
At the lake called Abarger,
At the head of the cold gorge,
They set it on watch, they say.
Of the leopard lord Manas,
At the place where he would come,
At the meeting of nine roads,
In the region of Börü-Koy,
On the jutting spur of Üzgültük mountain,
On the looming headland,
Beside Kara-Suu,
On the face of Kaspang-Too,
They set the wild ram on watch, they say.
From Karykan's throne,
They chose and brought it.
In Khan Esen's garden,
Teaching it human speech,
They had reared it when young.
It was a red fox forty fathoms long,
More watchful than other beasts,
A treasure belonging to Esenkan.
Is this not what made it a treasure?
The cunning fox set on watch
Was a support he relied upon.
No wind could match its trot,
No beast could match its stride.
It was calamity itself.
His many khans, led by Ezkara,
He gathered at his door, they say.
On this side of broad Altay,
Beyond broad Kara-Too,
Past the gold mine,
Where eight rivers meet,
Where eighty mountains come together,
On the rise of Seki-Moynok,
Upon the road where Manas would come,
He set the fox on watch, they say.
Hero Esenkan roused himself,
Making ready upon his throne.
People swarmed and seethed, filling the place.
Ay Jangjung and Kün Jangjung,
The companions beside him,
His confidants who offered counsel,
Were the ones standing close,
Soldiers swarmed and thronged,
People filled the place, seething.
Alöökö's Kongurbay,
Hero Kongurbay, the great grim-looking one,
When his champion entered,
Esen saw his arrival.
As soon as the grim one came,
Making him a house built on the upland,
Making him a mighty khan over the monks,
His tent with golden pillars,
His warrior, hero Kongurbay:
“Two reins and one lead-rope,
You are the son of hero Alöökö;
Now take them in your hands.
A fierce enemy hero has arisen;
From the Burut, lion Manas has arisen.
